::: {.report-kicker}
STAGE 02–04 / DIAGNOSIS, EXPERIMENT & POLICY
:::

::: {.report-summary}
**Which repurchase offer should be tested for which customers?**  
The decision is whether to send information, information plus a coupon, or no message to each customer. Sections 1–4 diagnose natural repurchase; sections 5–8 estimate average training-experiment effects; sections 9–12 independently evaluate a policy fixed on separate validation data. Incremental profit and side effects are assessed alongside reservation-budget and contact constraints.
:::


::: {.decision-box}
**Independent final evaluation of the selected policy:** incremental contribution profit per eligible customer **+282 KRW** (95% interval -154~+640 KRW), contact rate **28.1%**. Section 12 reports the final decision, including costs and upper confidence bounds for both side effects.
:::


::: {.data-stamp}
Self-generated synthetic data · Sections 1–8: training as of 2025-10-01 · Sections 9–12: validation 2026-03-01 / final 2026-08-01  
Assignment 14 days after first delivery → 60 days of additional payments → 30 further days for settlement  
Snapshot `sim-8aecf9722a5328b9`
:::

## 1. CRM eligibility and exclusions

Eligible customers made no additional payment during the 14 days after first delivery and meet first-order status, consent, and email requirements. Customers are randomized to no contact, information, or information plus a coupon. **The repurchase diagnosis in sections 1–4 uses only the no-contact arm.**

The 4,716 excluded customers include both customers who already repurchased and do not need this campaign and customers who do not meet contact requirements. They cannot all be interpreted as churned customers.

| Exclusion reason | Customers · overlaps allowed |
| --- | --- |
| Additional payment before assignment | 1,163 |
| No email consent | 2,873 |
| Email unavailable | 791 |
| First order fully refunded | 262 |

::: {.method-note}
The denominator consists of customers with confirmed first delivery whose scheduled D+14 assignment falls in the training period. Exclusion reasons can overlap, so their counts may not sum to the number of excluded customers.
:::

## 2. Cumulative repurchase by assignment month

Monthly differences reflect both customer composition and the synthetic generation rules, so this table cannot establish that a particular month's operations or content were more effective. A row remains NA if the full monthly cohort has not completed 90-day settlement.

## 3. Repurchase timing by customer group

Cumulative repurchase in the full control group reaches 50% at 36.4 days after assignment, or approximately 50.4 days after first delivery. The curves show **Kaplan–Meier cumulative repurchase, 1−S(t)**, incorporating time to first repurchase. Customers without a purchase remain in the denominator while observed and are right-censored at observation end.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

::: {.method-note}
The risk set comprises customers still observed who have not repurchased **immediately before** the stated time. Table values count customers. Customers whose follow-up ends at the 60-day boundary are included immediately before that boundary. Intervals are pointwise 95% Greenwood log-log intervals.
:::

::: {.decision-box}
**Planning implication:** natural repurchase timing can inform message scenarios. The sending day is fixed at D+14 in this experiment. A time read from these curves therefore cannot be established as the optimal sending day. Timing effects require a separate randomized experiment.
:::

## 4. Customer-group differences and next hypotheses

60-day repurchase by first package: 500g: 64.7%, 200g: 56.4%. The observed gap of 8.3 pp describes a customer-group difference. It does not mean that changing package size or sending a coupon would produce that improvement.

| First package | Settled customers | Repurchasers | 60-day repurchase | 95% interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 200g | 1,517 | 856 | 56.4% | 53.9%–58.9% |
| 500g | 1,845 | 1,194 | 64.7% | 62.5%–66.9% |
| 1,000g | 1,743 | 1,081 | 62.0% | 59.7%–64.3% |

Among the full control group of 5,105 customers, 3,131 repurchased, a rate of 61.3%, with a Wilson 95% interval of 60.0%–62.7%. First package size is observed before assignment, but may also reflect differences in purchase motivation, consumption, and other factors.

| Diagnostic question | Next comparison | Decision metric |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does information help groups with low natural repurchase? | D+14 information versus no contact; prespecified exploration by package size | 60-day incremental contribution profit and repurchase-rate difference |
| Are discounts reaching customers who would buy anyway? | Identical information plus coupon versus information alone | Incremental profit after coupon, shipping, and refund costs |
| Can targeting only low repurchase rates lose money? | Send-to-all, coupon-to-all, and customer-level policies | Validation incremental profit within budget; unsubscribe rate |

Sections 5–8 report average training-experiment effects; sections 9–12 connect these to customer-level allocation. Models use training customers only. The policy was selected and locked on validation data before evaluating separately generated final customers.


## 5. Three-arm assignment and baseline features

All **15,284 assigned training customers** completed the 60-day outcome window and 30-day settlement period. **ITT compares the full original assigned arms**, regardless of failed sends, unopened messages, or unused coupons. First-order profit is excluded.

Each arm was assigned with probability 1/3. The sample-ratio mismatch (SRM) test p-value is **0.8664**, above the investigation threshold of 0.001; no departure from the prespecified assignment ratio was detected. Independent reconciliation of the source ledger and marts matched customer-level accounts for all 15,284 customers.

The maximum absolute standardized mean difference (|SMD|) across the three pairwise comparisons of displayed baseline features is **0.058**; all displayed features are below the 0.1 reference. This diagnoses balance in observed features; it does not prove that randomization is perfect. Missingness in pre-assignment visit records was checked separately.

### Message delivery and usage

| Assigned arm | Assigned | Attempted | Reached | Opened | Redeemed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No contact | 5,105 | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| Information | 5,064 | 5,064 | 4,757 | 2,066 | Not applicable |
| Information + coupon | 5,115 | 5,115 | 4,808 | 1,980 | 837 |

Each cell counts customers. Unreached customers remain in the profit-comparison denominator. Opens and coupon redemption do not necessarily form a sequential funnel; effects are not calculated only among openers or redeemers.

## 6. Incremental contribution profit per customer

Each arm's 60-day contribution profit accounts for discounts, refunds, product costs, shipping, payment fees, and sending costs. Averages below are in **KRW per assigned customer**, distinct from total revenue or averages among purchasers only.

| Comparison | Incremental profit / assigned customer | Individual 95% interval | Holm-adjusted p | Interpretation within synthetic world |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Information − no contact | +888 KRW | +169~+1,608 KRW | 0.0156 | Evidence of an increase |
| Information + coupon − no contact | +2,199 KRW | +1,475~+2,922 KRW | <0.001 | Evidence of an increase |
| Information + coupon − information | +1,311 KRW | +577~+2,044 KRW | <0.001 | Evidence of an increase |

::: {.method-note}
Lines are Welch **individual 95% confidence intervals**, not simultaneous intervals for the three comparisons. Table p-values use Holm correction across the three prespecified contribution-profit comparisons.
:::

Incremental profit for information + coupon versus no contact is **+2,199 KRW/customer**, and the difference versus the same information alone is **+1,311 KRW/customer**. The added value of the coupon must be judged by directly comparing the information + coupon and information-only arms.

### Repurchase with the same ITT denominator

| Comparison | Repurchase-rate difference | Individual 95% interval · exploratory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Information − no contact | +1.19 pp | -0.70 pp~+3.07 pp |
| Information + coupon − no contact | +6.45 pp | +4.60 pp~+8.30 pp |
| Information + coupon − information | +5.26 pp | +3.41 pp~+7.11 pp |

Rate-difference intervals use the Newcombe score method and are secondary analyses. A higher repurchase rate alone does not establish profitability; contribution profit above is the primary metric.

## 7. Added coupon value and cost reconciliation

The waterfall sums per-customer accounting differences for **information + coupon − information**. Positive components increase the profit difference and negative components reduce it. The final total matches the experiment estimate of +1,311 KRW/customer above.

::: {.method-note}
Coupon discounts already enter the waterfall's merchandise revenue after discounts, so coupon cost is not deducted again. This is an accounting decomposition; components are not interpreted as independent causal mechanisms or mediation effects. The total profit-difference interval is reported above instead of component-level uncertainty.
:::

Among the coupon arm's 5,115 customers, 837 redeemed a coupon; actual CRM coupon discounts average **491 KRW per assigned customer**. Redeemed discounts differ from the KRW 3,000 budget reserved at issuance.

| Assigned arm | List-price merchandise | Other discounts | CRM coupon discounts | Revenue after discounts | Sending cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No contact | 34,133 KRW | 0 KRW | 0 KRW | 34,133 KRW | 0 KRW |
| Information | 36,114 KRW | 0 KRW | 0 KRW | 36,114 KRW | 20 KRW |
| Information + coupon | 40,174 KRW | 0 KRW | 491 KRW | 39,683 KRW | 20 KRW |

All table amounts are per assigned customer, with discounts and sending costs shown as positive expenditures. **List-price merchandise amount − other discounts − CRM coupon discounts = merchandise revenue after discounts.** Displayed amounts are rounded to whole KRW; calculations use unrounded means.

## 8. Side effects and operating conditions

Alongside profit, we assess increases in unsubscribe and refund-customer rates versus no contact. Tolerances are **+0.5 pp and +1.0 pp**, respectively. Decisions compare the uncertainty-adjusted upper bound with tolerance, rather than relying on the point estimate alone.

| Versus no contact | Metric | Observed increase | Adjusted one-sided upper bound | Tolerance | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Information | Unsubscribe | +0.16 pp | +0.54 pp | +0.50 pp | Not established |
| Information | Refund-customer rate | -0.10 pp | +0.81 pp | +1.00 pp | Within tolerance |
| Information + coupon | Unsubscribe | +0.72 pp | +1.17 pp | +0.50 pp | Not established |
| Information + coupon | Refund-customer rate | +0.44 pp | +1.38 pp | +1.00 pp | Not established |

A one-sided family alpha of 0.05 is divided across **4 comparisons** (two active arms × two metrics), giving **98.75% one-sided upper bounds**. Chart lines run from the estimate to the upper bound and differ from two-sided 95% intervals. “Not established” means the upper bound is not within tolerance; it does not establish that deterioration necessarily exceeds tolerance.

### Planning decision at this stage

| Option | Contribution profit vs no contact | Side-effect conditions | Planning decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Information | Evidence of an increase | Unsubscribe: tolerance not established | Modify operations and validate further |
| Information + coupon | Evidence of an increase | Unsubscribe·Refund-customer rate: tolerance not established | Modify operations and validate further |

::: {.decision-box}
The design caps contact at 30% of eligible customers and reserves up to KRW 3,000,000 in variable costs per 10,000 customers. **Profit, side effects, and operating constraints must be checked together.** These three-arm averages are not final customer-policy results, so an arm that sends everyone the same message is not approved as a final campaign satisfying those constraints.
:::

In the following policy stage, these results serve as baselines for selecting customers and benefits using pre-assignment features. Changes to content, frequency, or subscription preferences that could reduce contact burden are separate experimental hypotheses. Proposing real operational expansion requires independent evaluation of a locked policy and confirmation of side-effect conditions. Validation and final-evaluation data were not used in these arm comparisons.

### Experiment calculation and reproduction

Inputs are the same synthetic source as the diagnosis. Results are in `report/data/experiment.json`; assignment, balance, delivery, and accounting checks are in `report/data/experiment_checks.json`. The `compare-arms` command regenerates diagnostic and experiment charts together, and Quarto bundles them into one HTML file.

Mean inference refers to [SciPy Welch t-test](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.ttest_ind.html); independent proportion-difference intervals refer to the [Newcombe implementation](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.stats.proportion.confint_proportions_2indep.html). Independent pilot power simulation has not been performed. Sample size and seeds were not changed in response to these results.



## 9. Customer-level models and policy lock

Building on the three-arm average comparisons, 11 pre-assignment features predict **conditional contribution profit and side-effect probabilities** for no contact, information, and information plus coupon. Only the assigned treatment's outcome is observed for each customer. Model differences therefore estimate **conditional average effects**, not observed individual true effects.

| Purpose | Assignment dates | All assigned customers | Prespecified label cutoff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Training | 2025-01-15 inclusive–2025-07-01 exclusive | 15,284 | 2025-10-01 |
| Validation / selection | 2025-10-01 inclusive–2025-12-01 exclusive | 15,167 | 2026-03-01 |
| Locked-policy final evaluation | 2026-03-01 inclusive–2026-05-01 exclusive | 15,363 | 2026-08-01 |

Each split retains the full originally randomized population with completed 90-day settlement. Preprocessing and models are fitted on training data only; validation selects candidates, and the final split evaluates the locked policy only. Models, λ, and policies are not reselected after seeing final results.

### Two models and eight policy candidates

The training set contains **15,284 customers**. Candidates are Ridge(α=100) and histogram gradient boosting (HGB). A T-learner fits separate contribution-profit models for each arm; unsubscribe and refund outcomes are modeled as classification probabilities. Negative and 0 profit values are retained. Numeric imputation, scaling, and categorical encoding are fitted on training data only. Months/channels first appearing later are handled as unseen categories.

Applying reservation-cost penalties λ=0, 0.5, 1, 2 to each model gives 8 candidates for validation. Sending candidates are ranked by **predicted incremental profit − λ×reserved cost**. The λ penalty allocates scarce resources; it is not deducted as an accounting cost from evaluated contribution profit. All policies share prespecified HGB outcome predictions for DR evaluation, separating policy ranking models from the evaluation nuisance model.

The profit criterion requires the lower bound of the validation DR approximate 95% interval to exceed fixed setup cost per customer. Side-effect screening covers 8 candidates × 2 metrics and uses Bonferroni-corrected **99.6875% one-sided upper bounds**. Validation intervals are normal approximations for fixed action scores; they are not final inference accounting for all allocation dependence and selection optimism.

Among feasible candidates, prefer the simpler Ridge model if it lies within 1 standard error of the highest DR estimate. Within a model, rank by decreasing DR, increasing λ, then fixed identifier. Select no contact if no candidate is feasible. Validation yielded 4 feasible candidates, including 3 within 1 standard error. **HGB · λ=0.5** was selected and locked.

## 10. Independent incremental profit of the locked policy

The final denominator is **all 15,363 assigned customers**; the analysis does not retain only customers whose assigned arm matches the policy action. Actual randomization probabilities compare policy value with the value of no contact for everyone. DR combines outcome predictions with assignment probabilities as the primary analysis; IPW provides a probability-weighted check.

| Policy | DR incremental profit / customer | 95% interval · KRW | IPW check / customer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Locked policy: HGB · λ=0.5** | +282 KRW | -154~+640 | +290 KRW |
| Keep no contact | +0 KRW | +0~+0 | +0 KRW |
| Random information priority | +222 KRW | -173~+596 | +163 KRW |
| Random coupon priority | +127 KRW | -78~+363 | -174 KRW |
| Package/tips rule | +238 KRW | -66~+531 | -47 KRW |
| Non-repurchase risk priority | +243 KRW | +66~+457 | +332 KRW |

The locked policy's primary estimate is **+282 KRW/eligible customer**, with a 95% interval of **-154~+640 KRW**. The IPW check is +290 KRW, with an interval of -213~+798 KRW. Other rows are prespecified **exploratory baselines**. They are not used to choose a new final winner, nor to claim simultaneous superiority over multiple baselines.

For the same locked policy, DR incremental profit moved from +1,010.73 KRW/customer on validation to +281.94 KRW/customer on final data; the estimate decreased. Sampling variation, validation selection optimism, and customer-composition differences are possible explanations, but this comparison cannot separate or establish the cause.

Customers are resampled with replacement within assignment days for **2,000 bootstrap repetitions**. Repeated customers occupy separate slots; allocation and constraints are recalculated for the same policy in each repetition, without model refitting or policy reselection. The intervals therefore condition on the locked models/policy and observed daily composition, excluding full training uncertainty and uncertainty about generalization to real markets.

### Scaling to rollout size and accounting for costs

For **10,000 eligible customers**, scaled incremental profit after setup cost is **+2,719,396 KRW**, with an interval of **-1,636,266~+6,301,281 KRW**. The calculation is `DR incremental profit per customer × rollout population − fixed setup cost`; setup cost here is 100,000 KRW. Setup cost is charged only when at least one customer is contacted; the bootstrap reapplies this condition.

Discounts, refunds, product costs, shipping, payment, and sending costs already enter customer-level contribution profit. Reservation budgets and λ penalties are not deducted again. Scaling is a planning calculation conditional on unchanged customer composition and operating conditions, not a forecast of actual sales.

## 11. Constrained allocation and selection rationale

The contact cap is **30%** of eligible customers; the variable-cost reservation budget is **3,000,000 KRW per 10,000 customers**. Each assignment day's caps are proportional to its eligible population and rounded down to integers. Coupons reserve **full face value plus sending cost**, without discounting by expected redemption. Fixed setup cost of 100,000 KRW is accounted for separately, outside the variable-cost reservation cap.

The evaluation population receives 4,318 contacts (28.1%), against a total contact cap of 4,583. Reserved cost is **4,538,360 KRW**, against summed daily caps of 4,608,900 KRW. The original allocation has 0 violating days and the bootstrap has 0 violating repetitions: **All assignment-day constraints met**.

Actions with positive predicted incremental profit are allocated by score, with at most one action per customer. Only positive predicted increases in unsubscribe/refund risk are accumulated, so one customer's predicted risk reduction cannot offset another's predicted increase. This allocation filter does not replace the observed-outcome side-effect evaluation in the next section. The greedy implementation respects constraints but **does not guarantee a global optimum**.

The first-package table explains whom the locked policy selects. It does not establish true individual or segment-level causal effects. The non-repurchase risk baseline ranks the chance of not repurchasing, not the incremental response to a message. Random, rule, and risk baselines use the same contact, reservation-budget, predicted-risk filters, and positive incremental-profit requirement.

## 12. Side-effect upper bounds and final decision

The locked policy's unsubscribe and refund-customer rates are compared with no contact for everyone. Differences below are IPW estimates from observed labels, distinct from model-predicted risk scores.

A one-sided family α=0.05 across two metrics yields **97.50% one-sided upper bounds**. Their scope differs from the 4 comparisons in the arm-average analysis and from validation candidate screening. Intervals for multiple exploratory baselines do not provide simultaneous safety guarantees.

The number of IPW customers whose assigned arm matches the policy action is 5,195, with an effective sample size of 5,195.0. Matched counts and effective sample size diagnose weighted information; the analysis denominator remains 15,363 customers. Dependence on matched counts and the DR/IPW difference are assessed together.

::: {.decision-box}
**Modify operating conditions or collect more evidence.** Evidence is not yet sufficient to jointly establish the profit lower-bound, both side-effect, and resource criteria.
:::

The policy is not reoptimized on the same final split after observing its result. Revisions require a new experiment with separate customers and periods.

### Methods, records, and remaining validation

Public aggregates are in `report/data/policy.json`; prespecified rules are in `docs/STAGE_4_POLICY_SPEC.md`. The actual UTC execution time of policy locking differs from the synthetic business dates in the tables. File creation order is also checked to confirm that the lock precedes final-source generation. Independent pilot power simulations and repeated inference/false-expansion checks in A/A null-effect worlds remain incomplete.

Models refer to [scikit-learn Ridge](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.Ridge.html) and [HistGradientBoostingRegressor](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor.html); DR policy evaluation refers to [Dudík·Langford·Li, Doubly Robust Policy Evaluation and Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.4601).


## 13. Interpretation and scope

- **Synthetic world:** data follow prespecified generation assumptions, not actual consumer research or real-company/brand performance records. Statistical significance concerns mean differences within this fixed synthetic world and does not validate real-brand performance. The 95% intervals describe sampling uncertainty in that world, not the probability of success in a real market. Policy evaluation uses a wholly fictional RCT and does not authorize immediate sending for a real brand.
- **Population:** each analysis split includes eligible customers who have not repurchased by D+14. Results are not generalized to all first-time buyers or customers without consent.
- **Feature timing:** both event time and recorded time must precede assignment. Arm labels are metadata and are excluded from prediction features.
- **Outcome definition:** an additional payment remains a repurchase event even if later refunded. Contribution profit separately accounts for refunds, shipping, payment, and sending costs.
- **Window boundaries:** payments are counted in `[assignment, assignment+60 days)`; final records must precede assignment+90 days. Unsettled outcomes are not replaced with 0.
- **Analysis separation:** hidden generator traits (oracle) were not used. Sections 1–8 use training customers only, excluding validation and final customers.

### Reproduction and method references

The HTML version combines Plotly charts in Quarto as a single file containing scripts and styles; chart display works without an external CDN. Original aggregates are in `report/data/diagnostics.json`, input/code hashes in `report/data/analysis_manifest.json`, and mart-building code in `src/crm_retention_lab/marts.py`.

Statistical methods refer to [lifelines KaplanMeierFitter](https://lifelines.readthedocs.io/en/latest/fitters/univariate/KaplanMeierFitter.html); output construction refers to [Plotly HTML export](https://plotly.com/python/interactive-html-export/) and [Quarto HTML documents](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-basics.html). Implemented survival probabilities and intervals are independently cross-checked against lifelines.
